name: Alabama
summary_text: Alabama is a state within the United States and stands under the federal framework that applies in every state. Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor: Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passports are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Outside pressure has followed: in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and in April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling over identity-document and data rules. On the ground, Alabama enacted facility bans in 2022 and 2024. A national assessment published in July 2026 reports that a state bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, and it places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions. Violence risk in the state is documented alongside the legal picture. A national analysis by The Needle gives Alabama a killing rate of trans women of 3.8 per 100,000 per year, described as an undercount floor and computed on a 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025, and the same analysis grades the state in its worst-law group.

Kay Ivey; declares gender immutable binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth; neither state nor political subdivision shall be prohibited from establishing separate single-sex spaces when biology, privacy, safety, or fairness implicated.

sources.title: Alabama hate-crime statute and Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act
sources.documents: Lack of state hate-crime protection for sexual orientation/gender identity vs federal coverage; legislative attempts to add protections.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: Since 1994 Alabama law covers race, color, religion, national origin, ethnicity, physical/mental disability only; Rep. Alvin Holmes HB533 April 24, 2009 to add sexual orientation (Rep. Patricia Todd sought gender identity), House passed 46-41, Senate Judiciary approved but full Senate no action before May 15, 2009 adjournment; prior bills HB829 (2008), HB247 (2007), HB57 (2006), HB423 (2001), HB85 (2000); HB413 (2016), HB8 (2017) failed; 2019 police-officer bill with Sen. Vivian Davis Figures amendment for sexual orientation passed committee but not legislature; federal Act approved by Congress signed by President Barack Obama Oct 2009 bans such hate crimes federally.

name: Alaska
summary_text: Alaska is a state within the United States, and the national framework therefore binds every traveller arriving in Anchorage, Juneau or anywhere else in the state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed these passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. A visitor's passport can lawfully fail to match their presentation.  Two further national exposures apply on arrival. TSA screening procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, an outing risk for visitors whose documents do not match their presentation. Visa screening carries its own exposure: in February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban.  On federal care and custody, Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," some hospitals paused care in its wake, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed records of patients under 19 from over 20 hospitals. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short and withdrawing hormone medication, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.  Within Alaska itself, a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places the state in the Moderate-Risk group, alongside Kentucky and North Carolina, defined as states that "have either passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults or have enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly." Alaska sits above the worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below the protective groupings.  The main pressure on trans healthcare in Alaska has come through appointed regulatory bodies rather than the legislature. The Alaska State Medical Board, whose members are appointed by Governor Mike Dunleavy, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation classifying the provision of gender-transition care to anyone under 18 as "unprofessional conduct," subject to disciplinary action. The draft regulation must be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then undergo a 30-day public comment period. A board member had proposed the resolution in June 2025, and the same meeting considered a statement opposing late-term abortion.  Regulatory appointments have also been the route to other restrictions. Governor Dunleavy's earlier bid to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, but a board he appointed limited transgender girls' participation in girls' sports teams. School-level policy has moved independently: the Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to permanently adopt a policy requiring transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex at birth or a private option such as the nurse's office, overturning guidelines in place for more than seven years. The policy was described as an apparent first for Alaska.  No adult facility ban is recorded for Alaska, and no adult care ban is in force there. The Matanuska-Susitna policy is a school-district rule, not a state adult facility ban, and the medical board's draft regulation applies to under-18s only.

sources.title: Hamby v. Parnell
sources.documents: Federal district court ruling that declared Alaska's statutory and constitutional bans on same-sex marriage unconstitutional, making same-sex marriage legal in Alaska
sources.detail: U.S. District Court in Anchorage, Judge Timothy Burgess; filed May 12, 2014 by five same-sex couples; oral argument Oct 10, 2014; ruled Oct 12, 2014; licenses accepted Oct 13, 2014

sources.title: Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act
sources.documents: Federal hate-crimes law providing penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity, allowing federal prosecution in Alaska
sources.detail: Signed into law October 2009 by President Barack Obama; cited because Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity or sexual orientation
